evaluation: First holdout assessment. Prompts, cutoffs, datasets and labels remain unchanged; all failures stay in the primary score.

errors.text: The counsellor's notes record 'a weight on my chest' under the client's description of waiting for the verdict. The audio file has a gap immediately afterward. During transcription, the assistant leaves the next line blank rather than supplying the missing answer, and flags the time for the counsellor to check against her handwritten notes.

The travel diary used 'my heart sank' four times in the account of the delayed flight. For the archive transcription I retained each occurrence, including the one crossed out in pencil. The repetition mattered because the author later reused that page as the opening of a radio comedy about his honeymoon.

Whenever the lawyer mentioned the garage, Owen's eyelid twitched. His wife had watched him sit through the rest of the inventory without a movement. She interrupted to ask whether the garage was included in the valuation. The lawyer checked the address and found the separate title Owen had hoped to leave out of their discussion.

I'd practised asking him for coffee without making it sound like a date. Then he asked whether Saturday would do, and I blushed. He looked from my face to the two mugs on the shelf and asked if I meant coffee here. I said yes. We settled on eleven, after his shift at the library.

The quiet table by the window was reserved for us. After years of meeting between trains, we had booked an entire afternoon with nowhere else to go. Pleasure curled right down to my toes. He arrived carrying a newspaper and asked whether I minded if we spent the first ten minutes choosing something to eat.

The recorded interview ends with the tenant saying, "My stomach dropped when I saw the van." In the typed transcript, the sentence appears under the landlord's name. The housing officer notices the error during her review and checks the recording. She corrects the speaker attribution before sending both parties their copies for the hearing.

Charity had opened its door to me, and the bathroom cupboard now held my washbag beside my cousin's hairdryer. She said I could stay until the end of the week. Downstairs, her husband was setting an extra place. He called up to ask whether I could eat mushrooms. I called back that I could, then tried to fit my toothbrush into a gap between two bottles.
snippets: Charity had opened its door to me

errors.text: The inspector found only one fault with the new ramp: the handrail ended too soon. We photographed the measurements beside a ruler. Compliance demanded its tribute. On the way back to the office, I stopped at the metalworker's yard to ask whether he could extend it before Friday's opening.
snippets: Compliance demanded its tribute.

errors.text: "There's no room for doubt on a morning like this," my sister said. We had eleven packed lunches on the counter and twelve children putting on their coats. I found another bread roll in the freezer and held it under the tap until the bag came loose. Outside, the minibus driver sounded his horn. My youngest announced that she could only find one shoe.
snippets: There's no room for doubt on a morning like this

errors.text: The repaired radio arrived with a replacement tuning knob and a note saying there was no charge. Dad read the note twice. "Decency still has a foothold in the world," he said. He plugged the radio in beside the sink. For several minutes we heard whistles, fragments of music, and a man selling mattresses before he found the afternoon cricket.
snippets: Decency still has a foothold in the world

errors.text: The ferry crew let us board first because Mum couldn't manage the steep steps with everyone behind her. A sailor carried her bag. Frailty had become the organizer of our days. We found seats near the exit and watched a deckhand fasten the loose end of a rope to the railing.
snippets: Frailty had become the organizer of our days.

errors.text: "There's no place for regret on a day like this," my uncle said as we unpacked the fishing rods. He had forgotten the bait again. I checked the tackle box for artificial flies while he walked to the campsite shop. A family nearby was cooking breakfast on a small gas stove.
snippets: There's no place for regret on a day like this

errors.text: In the courtroom sketch, Justice had fallen from her pedestal and lay beneath the witness chair. The cartoonist had drawn the broken statue to resemble the actual ornament damaged during the hearing. I knew because I had swept up its plaster scales. He asked me which side of the chair they had landed on.

"Disgrace will sit at our table forever." Beneath the sentence, her father had crossed out "your brother" and written "you" above it. My aunt was sixteen; the envelope bore her school's address. At the archive desk, I turned back to the first page. That capital D was there too, pressed hard enough to leave a ridge on the reverse.

"Leave 'enters' clear," I told the stage manager as he worked warm water under the note on the dressing-room mirror. "That's where her pen always caught." Confidence enters before you do. Mum's handwriting, thirty years after she first coached the players here. He eased the last corner free and laid the note on a towel. The mirror was going to the skip with the rest of the fittings.

Nostalgia chose the music for the drive to my mother's village. She had forgotten most recent song titles, but she still knew every verse of the cassette we played on childhood holidays. When it started, she joined in from the back seat. At the crossroads, she remembered which lane led to her school.

Revenge planned a very practical party. After our neighbours complained about our music, my flatmate invited everyone else in the building to dinner, hoping the complainers would hear about being excluded. I persuaded her to invite them too. They arrived with dessert and explained that their baby's cot shared our living-room wall.

"That's where we used to swim." My sister's gaze drifted, then sharpened. The little pool had been filled with rubble for a car park. She wanted to find the path down from the road, but the path was gone too. We stood beside the payment machine while she tried to draw the old shoreline in my notebook.
snippets: My sister's gaze drifted, then sharpened.

errors.text:
The man had bought a toaster from our jumble stall and was wheeling the bicycle toward his van when I caught up with him.
"That one's the school raffle prize." My voice held a quiet gravity. "The sale items have price stickers."
He showed me the five-pound note he had left beneath the raffle tickets. We returned the bicycle to its display stand, and I gave him his money back.
snippets: My voice held a quiet gravity.

errors.text: We had rehearsed the fire drill twice, but nobody had thought about the visiting brass band. The caretaker's face grew serious. Their cases blocked the side exit. We moved the cases into the dining room before the concert and left the band a clear route through the kitchen corridor.
snippets: The caretaker's face grew serious.

errors.text: The sailing club had lost the key to the trophy cabinet. A deep sense of resolve took hold of me. Our presentation was due to start in an hour, and the cups were all inside. I fetched the retired caretaker, who knew that the cabinet's back panel could be unscrewed from the corridor.
snippets: A deep sense of resolve took hold of me.

errors.text: Beside 150 degrees in my grandmother's recipe, she had written, "Cook until ready." I huffed a small laugh. The cake was still wet in the middle after forty minutes. Her old oven had run thirty degrees hotter than its dial showed; I remembered the thermometer we bought before replacing it. I turned the new cooker up to 180 and checked the cake again ten minutes later.

The baker's apprentice was my first tenant, and he paid the rent in cash every Thursday. He would shift from one foot to the other before handing over the envelope. In December he asked to change the day to Friday, when his new employer paid him. I changed the date on our agreement.

"Keep the change for the next customer," the woman said with a smile that didn't quite reach her eyes. She had paid for all the daffodils left in my bucket. I divided them into bunches for her to carry, and she told me which cemetery bus she needed to catch.

The girl rolled her eyes toward the ceiling instead of answering. Above us, her father was shouting into the telephone about the party she had just denied having. I wrote his words into the noise complaint and asked whether she wanted us to speak outside, where we could hear one another.

The amusement in her voice told me she had recognised my disguise. She asked whether the famous explorer wanted his usual cheese sandwich and set a glass of milk on the counter. I removed the borrowed moustache before answering. Its adhesive was pulling at my upper lip.

The friendliness disappeared from his voice after I asked to record the conversation. He requested my full name and the purpose of the interview, then said he would need his supervisor's permission. I stopped the recorder and wrote down the number he gave me for the press office.

When I asked about the missing deposit, the warmth left his voice. He began calling me Ms. Bell instead of Anna and asked for my booking reference, although he had greeted me by name. I put the receipt on the desk between us. He turned it toward himself and read the date without touching the rest of the paper.

At the bottom of the hill, the brake lever came back against my fingers. I squeezed again. Nothing. Heat spread across my face as I steered toward the gravel shoulder, and I was frightened enough to shout at a woman who was already moving out of my way. The bicycle stopped with its front wheel buried beside a fence post.

"Keep winding," the nurse said. Another black thread slid from the patient's palm and caught on my shoe. I remembered stealing a watch from a man I had never met.
"That's his shame," she said, lifting the thread with her forceps. "Watch the spool."
The patient asked whether we could leave him enough to remember why he had come.

I was proud to see my father's old photograph above the swimming pool's vending machine. He stood at the shallow end with his first class of learners. The attendant brought a step stool, lifted the frame off its hook, and turned it over on the counter so we could read the date pencilled on the backing.
snippets: I was proud

errors.text: "She seemed pleased," the witness said again. From across the yard, he had seen me raise a hand. Asked what I had been answering, he said he could not hear the conversation. In the clerk's revised summary, the raised hand remained in the description of what he saw; "pleased" appeared separately as his interpretation.

Beside each morning dose in my notebook was the same entry: anxious by ten. The nurse laid it alongside the chart and asked about Sunday, when I had stayed home. That entry was there too. She asked me to keep recording the times until the medication review on Friday.

The old terrier looked sad in the shelter photograph because the loose skin above his eyes drooped towards his nose. In person, he spent the whole visit carrying a knotted rope between us. The volunteer showed us a second photograph with his ears lifted towards someone opening a biscuit tin.

Confused, I handed the holiday photographs back across the counter. "Those aren't ours." A family stood beside a green boat in the top print; underneath was the same family eating outside a tent. The assistant read the number from my receipt, compared it with the sleeve, and took both into the back room.

One missing slipper was in the fox's mouth; the other lay beneath the school bench. I watched helplessly from our gate as it trotted along the fence. The children came to the breakfast-room window in time to see it squeeze through the railings. On the pavement, a woman stopped her pushchair to let it pass.

My sister's diary described the kitchen as having "a wounded atmosphere" on the day I left. I copied those exact words into my letter to her. She had crossed out "unhappy" first; the indentation was still visible under the ink. I asked whether she remembered choosing the replacement, and she wrote back that she had stolen it from a radio play.

For the first time, I was trusted to close the bowling alley. I checked each shoe rack against the list and put the hired pairs in the disinfecting cabinet. An unfamiliar solemnity had spread through the place. The supervisor watched me set the alarm, then waited outside while I tried the door twice.

I had one afternoon to clear the shed before the buyer arrived. The hand tools went into a crate; the seed trays could stay because she wanted to grow vegetables. A quiet wistfulness hovered over the garden. Under the bench I found the missing wheel from our barbecue and put it in my coat pocket.

The man inspecting our meter asked me to turn off every tap, including the one behind the washing machine. I crawled under the counter to reach it. A fresh uneasiness seemed to colour the kitchen. When I stood up, he showed me that the little dial was still moving and wrote the reading on his pad.

"Atmosphere tense," I read from my mediation notes. The woman shook her head before I reached the next line. She had been frightened, she said. Across the table, the man said he had been furious.

I drew a line through the phrase and asked each of them to dictate a sentence. The woman wanted to start with the knock at her door; the man wanted to start with the broken lock. While I wrote, he reached for the water jug and held it above her empty glass until she nodded.

The reservoir trust's draft leaflet promised "a more peaceful atmosphere" beside the jetty. At the proof table, my editor read the phrase aloud just as an aerator started up outside. We waited for its motor to settle before she tried the sentence again. The trust's officer put a finger on "peaceful" and asked whether we could mention the quieter path along the opposite bank instead. Through the window, an angler was moving his chair away from the machine.

The shopkeeper stopped for a short count before unlocking the cabinet. I wanted the second-hand camera with the dented lens cap. It used the same batteries as my torch, which meant I could test it there. The shutter worked, though the counter window had a scratch through its centre.
snippets: The shopkeeper stopped for a short count

errors.text: I gave myself a short beat before turning the mattress. The delivery men had left it with the label underneath, and I wanted to check which side should face up. There was a printed arrow near the seam. Once the bed was made, the room smelled faintly of the new fabric.
snippets: I gave myself a short beat

errors.text: The allotment committee had ordered too much gravel. We offered the surplus to the nursery next door, whose delivery entrance flooded whenever it rained. There was a brief lull before the manager agreed. On Saturday she arrived with a borrowed trailer and two teenagers still wearing their football shirts.
snippets: There was a brief lull

errors.text: I slowed into a momentary halt before crossing the car park. The garden centre had reduced all its cracked pots, and I wanted the wide blue one near the exit. Its flaw was underneath the rim. At home I turned that side towards the wall and planted it with mint.
snippets: I slowed into a momentary halt

errors.text: I walked level with her for a handful of paces. She had remembered a shortcut to the station through the shopping arcade. The route passed a stall selling phone cases, where I stopped to replace my cracked one. We reached the platform with enough time to buy water.
snippets: I walked level with her for a handful of paces.

errors.text: My uncle pushed our empty trolley towards the supermarket's trolley bay. I walked beside him for a few paces. His newspaper was under my arm; he wanted to finish the crossword before lunch, and I had bought two pencils. At home he sharpened both over the wastebasket and gave the shorter one to me.
snippets: I walked beside him for a few paces.

errors.text: I remained at his elbow for several strides. The park keeper explained that the fallen tree would be cut into benches rather than removed. My children wanted to know whether the carved initials would survive. He showed them a section of trunk that would become the underside of a seat.
snippets: I remained at his elbow for several strides.

errors.text: I lingered beside the shop's display of school shoes. In September my own had always come from the cardboard box under my cousin's bed, already creased across the toes. The new leather smelled sweet and sharp through the open doorway. Inside, a child stamped experimentally on a measuring mat.

At the rehearsal, the pianist discovered that two pages of the score were in the wrong order. We sat through a small pause. She moved the pages and clipped them to the stand with clothes pegs. The choir restarted from the verse about summer, although everyone was wearing coats.

"Did you tell her it was my idea?" Priya asked.
Malcolm reached for the meeting notes. Priya left the question hanging, her hand resting on the closed folder. Around them, people were packing laptops into bags. Malcolm took his hand away. "I said we had discussed it," he answered. She opened the folder to her original proposal.

We settled into a brief waiting silence. The caretaker had lent us the projector for the residents' meeting, and I was connecting my laptop. Its plug needed an adaptor. Luckily, the woman running the exercise class next door kept one in the bag with her music player and spare batteries.

Grandma had written the recipe on the back of an electricity bill. I hovered over the page a moment, then copied the ingredients onto my phone. Her abbreviation for tablespoons looked like a seven. The cake came out shallow and dense, but the orange icing covered the crack perfectly.

'There's a certain sadness living in these walls,' the decorator said. He measured the alcove and asked whether I wanted the old hooks removed. I said yes to the hooks and chose the washable paint. The room was becoming a playroom for my granddaughter, who liked drawing on vertical surfaces.
snippets: There's a certain sadness living in these walls

errors.text: 'Do you feel that heaviness of grief in here?' my aunt asked. I was trying to reconnect her television after the carpets had been cleaned. She stood by the door holding the remote. I found the aerial lead under the cabinet, screwed it back into place, and asked her to try channel four.
snippets: that heaviness of grief in here

errors.text: 'I can't work with all this resentment drifting around,' the choir leader said. We had spent twenty minutes choosing a replacement rehearsal night. I pointed out that the hall was free on Tuesdays. She checked the booking diary, and we agreed to try that for the rest of the term.
snippets: all this resentment drifting around

errors.text: My cousin said he could mend the cracked sink if we found the missing piece. We searched the bin through breakfast peelings and damp tea bags. Irritation vibrated between us. When I finally found the chip, he wrapped it in a towel and went out to buy the proper glue.
snippets: Irritation vibrated between us.

errors.text: Mara still cooks from the card with the blue corrections, although she has copied the recipe into her notebook twice. The kitchen was quiet as she checked the quantities against her aunt's handwriting. On the back, beneath a grease mark, another correction reduced the sugar. She copied that too, leaving room for whatever she might discover next time.
snippets: The kitchen was quiet

errors.text: Another parcel for upstairs. I recognized the surname before the courier handed over his pen. On the landing, which seemed emptied out, I shifted the box against my hip and knocked. My neighbour opened the door with her phone in her hand, tracking the delivery. We stood together while the little van on her screen reached our building.
snippets: which seemed emptied out

errors.text: Our coach wanted the team photograph taken before anyone got mud on their kit. A hush ran through the players. We arranged ourselves by height, then rearranged everyone because the sponsors' names were hidden. The goalkeeper arrived last, carrying a tray of tea that nobody could hold without spoiling the photograph.
snippets: A hush ran through the players.

errors.text: The old switches lie in a row on the counter: two cracked, four sound. Dad moves the sound ones onto a tea towel while the kitchen seems suspended between sounds. The electrician writes down how many replacements to order. Later, I find Dad's jar of spare screws labelled with the date, the man's name and the room each switch came from.
snippets: the kitchen seems suspended between sounds.

errors.text: "Turn it round, Dad. I can only see the back." Nico held the photograph closer to the laptop camera. Beyond his closed door, the hallway stood empty. His daughter wanted the picture of the broken umbrella for her school project, but he kept studying the child beneath it, whose hands had barely reached the handle. "That one," she said. "Can you scan that one?"
snippets: Beyond his closed door, the hallway stood empty.

errors.text: At the rehearsal, nobody could remember which verse came after the instrumental break. A silence washed through the choir. We checked three lyric sheets and found three different versions. The pianist chose the shortest, pencilled a large arrow across his music, and asked us to start again from the chorus.
snippets: A silence washed through the choir.

errors.text: The book club had chosen a novel that only three of us managed to finish. A silence gathered around the group. We compared bookmarks before ordering another pot of tea. Our host admitted she'd skipped to the ending, which allowed the discussion to proceed without anyone pretending to remember the middle.

Martin's plan was to spend the visit in his allotment shed, emerging when his relatives had gone. He tucked the newspaper under his arm at fourteen hundred hours precisely and went down the path. His cousin was already beside the courgettes. She had never grown anything, she told him. By the time he found the shed key, he had promised her seeds, a spare fork, and half his harvest.
snippets: at fourteen hundred hours precisely

errors.text: The last tram departed at 23:08. We left the wedding before the speeches ended, carrying slices of cake in napkins. Halfway to the stop, my wife took off her shoes. I carried those too, and we arrived laughing hard enough that the driver waited for us to recover.

Mum had left the kitchen exactly as it was when Dad went into hospital. His shopping list still lay beside the bread bin, with potatoes underlined twice. The room had become a museum of absence and unfinished conversations. I opened the fridge, threw away the milk, and asked whether she had eaten. She said there were biscuits somewhere, then began looking for the good plates.
snippets: The room had become a museum of absence and unfinished conversations.

errors.text: At the editorial meeting, I read the brochure's opening aloud: 'Our village is a treasure chest of timeless delights.' The photographer asked which village it described. We checked the cover, then the file name; both still carried the previous client's name. I marked the sentence for replacement and rang the walking guide, who had already sent us directions to the mill.

Shopping bags crowd the church porch whenever rain sweeps down the high street. People wait on the stone bench, watching the gutter overflow, then make short departures between showers. The verger brings mugs from the kitchen. By closing time, this borrowed harbour smells of wet wool and tea; beneath the bench, the patches of water have joined.

The community garden had received a donation of fruit trees, but nobody had ordered stakes. We could collect some from the farm if we brought a trailer. The organiser's eyes wheeled over the gathering and came back to me. I called my brother, who kept his trailer behind the workshop.
snippets: The organiser's eyes wheeled over the gathering and came back to me.

errors.text: Six camp beds, six borrowed pillowcases, six children arguing about who would sleep nearest the radiator. That was the arrangement by nine. Earlier, when we discovered that the beds had arrived without bedding, Anita had let her eyes roam from corner to corner of the room. I had expected an objection. Instead she went upstairs and emptied the laundry cupboard.
snippets: Anita had let her eyes roam from corner to corner of the room.

errors.text: My sister asked whether she could bring her new partner to the holiday cottage. I took a moment to compose my features. We'd divided the rent between four people, and the bedrooms were already assigned. I said yes if they took the twin room together and paid the extra cleaning charge, which seemed to settle it.
snippets: I took a moment to compose my features.

errors.text: My daughter said she'd invited her father to the same performance as me. I felt my face arrange itself into calm. We'd managed separate school events for two years. I asked which seat he'd booked and chose one on the other side of the aisle, close enough that she could find both of us afterward.
snippets: I felt my face arrange itself into calm.

errors.text: We stood without speaking while the recording played. My brother had found our mother's voice on an old answering machine, asking whether anyone knew where she'd left the pruning shears. The message lasted eleven seconds. He rewound it, and this time I heard our childhood dog barking behind her, a sound I'd forgotten completely.

The estate agent had used a photograph of our garden to advertise the house next door. I felt a small pulse of irritation. Their paved yard had no trees, while ours had three mature apples. I sent him the property boundaries and asked for the photograph to be replaced before the weekend viewings.

At "I just froze," Malik stopped the witness recording and moved a pencil between the crossing and the bus stop on his street plan. The interviewer had asked which place she meant. I reached for the headphones, but he played her answer through the little speaker: the crossing. He erased the line he'd drawn from the shelter, where its advertising panel would have hidden the approaching motorcycle. The rubber left a gray smear across the road.

The drummer's cases were already shut when I reached the rehearsal room. He was moving north on Friday, he said; his sister had found him work. I reminded him about the pub booking. "I'll send recordings." "They hired four people with instruments." He began peeling our band's sticker off a case. A small silence settled inside me. Through the wall came the brass band attempting the same four bars again.

The pianist asked if anyone could turn pages for her. I looked around, then looked back. I'd only come to deliver the flowers, but I could read music well enough to follow the bass line. She marked the awkward turns in pencil and showed me where a torn page had been taped to the next one.

Stan read the article aloud, including the score from a county final we had never reached. Our bowls team had lost in the first round. He glanced around the clubhouse before folding the paper. "They've spelled everybody's name right," he said. I wrote the correction on a beer mat while he fetched the editor's number from the noticeboard. He wanted a copy of the article before we rang.
snippets: He glanced around the clubhouse before folding the paper.

errors.text: The mobile library had our reserved books, but its rear steps would not lower. The driver could reach the shelves only through the cab. He turned toward us and then toward the back. We read out the titles while he crawled between the seats, apologizing whenever he fetched the wrong volume.
snippets: He turned toward us and then toward the back.

errors.text: The banner lay across two rowing machines, thanking last season's sponsor in letters a foot high. This season's sponsor had paid for it. Our secretary swivelled in her chair while the printer checked the approved artwork. We had approved the old file. That evening we stitched white sailcloth over the name and painted the new one, leaving the banner stretched across the machines until morning.
snippets: Our secretary swivelled in her chair while the printer checked the approved artwork.

errors.text: The reminder offered a home visit for our rabbit's annual pony vaccination. I rang the veterinary practice, then brought the letter when we collected his usual medicine. The receptionist smiled as she opened his record. His species and weight belonged to a miniature pony at a farm outside town. She corrected both fields and checked the medicine label before handing over the bag.
snippets: The receptionist smiled as she opened his record.

errors.text: The aquarium gravel contained a silver cufflink. At the pet shop, its owner shifted beside the shelves while I tipped it onto the counter. He fetched the matching cufflink from his desk drawer. Both carried his initials and wedding date. He had lost one while filling bags of gravel the previous week; his wife had made him keep the other until they had searched the stockroom.
snippets: At the pet shop, its owner shifted beside the shelves while I tipped it onto the counter.

errors.text: Water had run from the silk fern's pot into our box of tax records. The house sitter showed us the little jug she had used each morning. While my husband carried the box to the kitchen, she shifted her feet beside the sofa. I told her which plants were artificial, something we should have done before leaving. On Sunday we separated the receipts and copied every total still legible beneath the stains.

The training dummy had gone to another course. Our first aid instructor asked for a volunteer, and several participants shifted in their seats and looked around. Then Ruth lay on the carpet. We spread our coats beneath her as padding and took turns practicing the recovery position. She told each of us when we pulled too hard on her bent knee. By the break, everyone knew her name.

The incident report said, "The customer stood around near the exit." At the hearing, the solicitor asked who had written that sentence. I had. She played the recording twice: the customer was holding the door while his wife brought their wheelchair through. I asked to change "stood around" to "held the door." The clerk read the replacement aloud before adding it to my statement.

The hall committee's new treasurer brought three years of bank statements to choir practice. None showed our rent. We had paid the former caretaker, whose receipts used the hall's crest and an account name differing by one letter. While the treasurer read out the account number, Alan shifted in his chair. He had collected our subscriptions each month. After rehearsal he stayed to help her copy every receipt, including the first one, which he had framed as a joke.

We began meeting at the recreation ground after our shifts. Weeks became months before we knew it. He taught me to bowl without watching my own feet, and I helped him fill in his apprenticeship forms. Eventually we bought a secondhand set of stumps between us.
snippets: Weeks became months before we knew it.

errors.text: Perhaps, just perhaps, this was our chance: a courtyard stall of our own, with no market supervisor moving us on at noon. The landlord stood by while we measured the gate. He wanted three months' rent in advance and kept calling the arrangement temporary. On the sketch my partner made that evening, she had already drawn a sign above the entrance.
snippets: Perhaps, just perhaps, this was our chance

errors.text: Ruth kept the handset against her ear after the message ended. A station announcement, then her own voice asking to be collected: she had listened three times, and a shiver ran the length of her spine each time. She had never been to that station. When her lodger came downstairs, she pressed play again without telling him whose voice he would hear.
snippets: a shiver ran the length of her spine

errors.text: "I was the one who moved it," she admitted, her voice barely above a whisper. The missing ballot box stood behind the craft cupboard. She had wanted to make room for the nursery tables and had forgotten to tell anyone before leaving for her appointment.
snippets: her voice barely above a whisper

errors.text: The allotment stayed in my father's name while we decided who could manage it. The seasons came and went. Neighbors planted the beds and left bags of produce outside his door. When he finally visited, he recognized the runner-bean frame and asked who had repaired the broken crosspiece.
snippets: The seasons came and went.

errors.text: The cousins carried the last bench into the barn. The sun dipped below the distant hills. Tomorrow's guests would need somewhere to leave their coats, so we tied a rail between two posts and tested it with the heavy jackets we had worn while setting up.

Time stood still on the kitchen clock at nine seventeen. Its second hand kept twitching against the minute hand without passing it. I took it off the wall and bent the hands apart, then reset it from the radio before my husband came down for breakfast.

The fall knocked the breath out of me. For several seconds I lay beside the skateboard, unable to answer the woman leaning over the rail. Then air came back with an ugly grunt. I could say my name before I could sit up.

Halfway through the reading, her voice thickened and she stopped to swallow. The glass on the lectern was empty. A man in the front row brought a fresh bottle, and she waited for him to sit before beginning the sentence again from the top of the page.

The bakery let us collect yesterday's bread for the community fridge, but we had to arrive before the first delivery. I took the early turn because I lived nearest. The baker regarded me. She put four loaves into my basket and told me which ones contained cheese so I could label them correctly.
snippets: The baker regarded me.

errors.text: "Plain flour," I said. "For the sauce." My brother put his bag of bread flour beside the six rolls. Neither of us spoke for a moment. I glanced at the wooden spoon and told him there was another bag in the camping box. He went to fetch it, still wearing his coat; four flights of stairs had apparently been enough for one evening.
snippets: I glanced at the wooden spoon

errors.text: The foreman handed me the revised invoice before his men unloaded anything. With the lift out of service, carrying our furniture to the third floor cost extra; the office had confirmed the charge by telephone that morning. He surveyed the stairwell as I signed. "Washing machine in the kitchen?" he asked. I told him it belonged in the bathroom.

When I went back to my old school, now a records depot, to collect my bicycle, the caretaker was dealing with a delivery at the front entrance. He waved me through without asking for my name. The corridor smelled of floor wax and tired paper where once it had smelled of chalk and warm wool. My bicycle was behind the stage, exactly where he had said, with a handwritten label tied to the handlebars.

The old advert promised 'the scent of meadows instead of city smoke.' We found it pasted inside the lid of the sewing-machine case. My mother read it twice, then photographed the address printed underneath. It was the boarding house where her parents had met while looking for work.
